Phison is serious about enterprise storage, and the Pascari X201P was not released lightly; it came in the night, under NDA, alongside this week’s Supercomputing 2026 event. The drive is part of the Performance X-Series, which handles intensive workloads where consistency is the name of the game. We were nevertheless pleasantly surprised by its write performance, with a steady 12 GB/s for sequential and over 600,000 random write IOPS, considering it’s marketed at the 1 drive write per day (DWPD) endurance point.

Part of that surprise comes from the fact that this is Phison’s read-intensive PCIe 5.0 data center drive, a successor to the X200P. It comes in the U.2 form factor — which can be more convenient in many cases — from 1.92TB to 30.72TB, and an E3.S version from 3.84TB, in both single- and dual-port models. It stands next to its mixed-use sibling, the X201E, which is the one rated for 3 DWPD. What makes the X201P exciting, in part, is its own 16-channel X2 controller and the flash that’s inside.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware This drive is aimed at AI, analytics, and database servers, with its case made in the 4K 70/30 mix at higher queue depths. It passed Phison’s one-million-IOPS mark at QD128 in our testing of the 15.36TB model, and the drive met all of its rated specs, though its random read rating required polled I/O to reach on our bench. It faced challenges with QD1 writes, log commits, and the middle range of our mixed sweeps. Given its blend of performance, capacity, and endurance, we consider it a very competent entry from the company that was perhaps better known in the consumer SSD market until recently.

The drive met or beat every rated performance figure that we can test, which should be the target of any enterprise SSD released today. If there’s an exception, it’s due to how we test; Phison lists a ceiling of 3,250K IOPS for 4K random read, which is higher than our bench allows with our interrupt-driven I/O, which we use rather than a polled approach. We also run a polled test on every drive for cases like this, and our result was 3,283K IOPS at the same queue depth Phison specifies, which shows the drive does exceed its specification.

Phison Pascari X201P: A Closer Look 

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Our sample is in the U.2 form factor, 15mm thick. We have the single-port SKU, ISE model XP208H0815T3P3216T310, with firmware X2WM6026. Some data we previously saw from the drive was reportedly on X2WM6025, but we confirmed X2WM6026 for all relevant results. We mounted the drive on a PCIe 5.0 x4 add-in card adapter for U.2, standing upright in the slot.

Phison did not provide firm hardware details, but we were able to discover some things on our own. The flash was probably the easiest, as the company claimed it was a 321-layer part. That can only be SK hynix’s V9 TLC, which is not flash we’ve tested before in any product. It’s exceptionally fast and uses a three-deck design, which is relatively new for TLC flash. The flash could be credited with some of the exceptional performance measurements we see on the drive.

As for the proprietary controller, we’ve heard that it’s using a combination of the standard Arm Cortex-R5 — these would be the main cores — with AndesCore RISC-V on the side. We’ve seen the latter before on the Phison E28 consumer SSD controller, which did have some enterprise-like aspects to it. The E28 is the newer design, built on a 6nm process with Andes’ newer N45 cores alongside the N25F, while the X2 is a 12nm part that, as far as we can tell, sticks with N25F-class co-processors.

In this case, the X2 has twice the flash channels, which enables a superior level of performance out of TLC flash, as in enterprise you do not rely on pSLC. That mix of cores sets the X2 apart from other 16-channel PCIe 5.0 enterprise controllers: Marvell’s Bravera SC5 and Silicon Motion’s SM8366 rely on Arm cores throughout, whereas Phison pairs its Cortex-R5 cores with small RISC-V co-processors.

Comparison Products

The comparison drive today is the Kioxia CD9P-R 7.68TB in the E3.S form factor. It is the first drive we tested in our new enterprise SSD review suite, and is a good comparison despite its smaller capacity, as it’s also a 1 DWPD, read-intensive PCIe 5.0 TLC drive. We tested both with 512-byte sectors. The form factor is different, which shouldn’t affect performance, though it could play a part in the temperature results. You can read the finer details of our test environment in our How we test enterprise SSDs article.

We did re-test the Pascari on three sweep points where our initial results deviated from expectations, and this is something our test is designed to detect. The charts use the re-measured results for those three points.

Performance at a Glance

These charts summarize the results that follow. The radar chart is scaled to the drives in this review, so its shape can’t be compared across reviews, and its 70/30 axis is the 4K mix at QD16. Latency is P99 at QD1, rather than an average, and on the relative chart, lower latency is drawn as a taller bar.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The X201P leads in several areas, most of all with writes: it is 65% ahead on sequential writes and 28% ahead on 4K random writes. 4K random reads are 11% ahead, and QD1 reads at P99 are 5% faster.

It trails on QD1 write latency at that same P99, though, at 10.0 versus 6.2 µs, with the CD9P-R’s 38% lower. The 4K 70/30 mix at QD16 has it about 6% behind, too. The drives are more or less the same with sequential read, because they are both at the 15 GB/s link limit. The most important gaps are the writes: these are large enough to lean towards the X201P for write-heavy work. The read-side gaps, meanwhile, are more modest.

Headline Performance — Four Corners 

Four corners testing covers the four headline numbers on an SSD spec sheet: sequential reads and writes, plus 4K random reads and writes. We test sequential transfers at 128K and 1MB with a queue depth (QD) of 64, and 4K random at QD256, split across eight fio jobs, since a single job can’t keep up with faster drives. On the fastest drives, the 4K random read result is capped by our bench rather than the drive, which is described in our testing notes and is covered by our polled test section further down.

Each test runs in the state the drive would be in after a long stretch of that kind of workload: the random tests start only after the drive passes our steady-state check, and we repeat the 4K write hours later to make sure it holds. The sequential tests, similarly, follow a full sequential fill. The results show what a drive sustains rather than what it manages fresh out of the box.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware The X201P is about 1.3% over its rating on three of the four corners, and is also ahead of the CD9P-R on three of four. Sequential read is a tie because, again, this is the limit of the PCIe 5.0 interface. The biggest gaps remain the writes: 12 GB/s versus 7.2 GB/s, and 608K versus 476K IOPS.

The random read corner is misleading because our interrupt-driven bench holds the X201P to 2.83 million IOPS, under its 3.25 million rating, but the X201P wins with or without the polling switch. One caveat here is capacity: at a 1:1 7.68TB, the X201P would likely lead less on writes, going by Phison’s own ratings for that model. The repeated 4K random write, hours later, matched the first at 608K IOPS.

Sequential Performance — Queue Depth Sweep

Sequential speed depends significantly on how much work is queued up. A single restore, scan, or file copy may keep only a few requests in flight, while a busy server can build up hundreds. We test 128K and 1MB sequential reads and writes at 11 different queue depths, from QD1 to QD1024, to see where each drive reaches full speed.

Beforehand, we erase the drive and write it end-to-end with 128K sequential writes, because sequential results on a drive full of random data can otherwise swing unpredictably from one queue depth to the next. The 1MB block size matches the transfers in our AI checkpoint and four corners tests.

Tom's Hardware Tom's Hardware Writes are the X201P’s best sequential result. It reaches full speed, near 12 GB/s, by QD2 with 1MB transfers and by QD4 with 128K, then stays there. That’s 65% faster than the CD9P-R at every depth past QD2.

While both drives top out at the interface limit for sequential read, they get there differently. With a single 128K stream, the X201P reads at 5.0 GB/s, which is more than double the CD9P-R. That may point to read-ahead. After that, the X201P stalls around 8.3 to 8.6 GB/s, from QD2 to QD8, needing QD32 for full speed; Phison’s own data also shows this. The CD9P-R gets full steam by QD16, giving it the edge there and at QD8. At the deeper end with 1MB reads, which the charts don’t show, the X201P holds its full speed where the CD9P-R drops off, by 6% at QD512 and 13% at QD1024.

Random Performance — Queue Depth Sweep 

Random performance changes dramatically with load. At QD1, with one request at a time, the result reflects the latency that single-threaded and latency-sensitive software feels most. At high queue depths, it shows how much work the drive can absorb from many users and jobs at once.
